and Bifacial Ag(In,Ga)Se2 Solar Cells
Jan Keller
| Sapna Mudgal | Natalia M. Martin | Olivier Donzel-Gargand | Marika Edoff
Ångström Laboratory, Division of Solar Cell Technology, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden
Correspondence: Jan Keller (jan.keller@angstrom.uu.se)
Received: 4 June 2025 | Revised: 17 June 2025 | Accepted: 20 June 2025

Keywords: AIGS | bifacial solar cell | CIGS | RbF-PDT | wide-gap chalcopyrite
ABSTRACT
This study investigates the impact of a RbF post-deposition treatment (PDT) on the properties of Cu-free, wide-gap (EG = 1.5 eV)
Ag(In,Ga)Se2 (AIGS) solar cells with either opaque Mo or transparent In2O3:W back contacts. The formation of a Rb-In-Se surface
phase and Cd in-diffusion from the buffer into this layer are detected. In addition, Rb is mainly located in Ag-depleted and In-
enriched grain boundaries and at the back interface. The RbF-PDT leads to decreased fill factor (FF) values, without providing any
gain in open-circuit voltage (VOC). This FF deterioration is more pronounced when a In2O3:W back contact is used. It is suggested
that transport barriers form at the Rb-In-Se/AIGS front and at the AIGS/GaOx/In2O3:W back interfaces after RbF-PDT. In addi-
tion, the GaOx thickness at the rear electrode increases. The absence of a VOC boost may be explained by the missing doping
increase after the RbF-PDT. Lastly, the AIGS solar cells from this study show slightly lower efficiencies as compared to Cu-
containing devices with the same EG but higher Ga content. However, the collection at rear illumination is marginally improved,
reaching up to 72% bifaciality in short-circuit current for the best cell with an In2O3:W back contact.
1 | Introduction
Today, the incorporation of the heavy alkali (HA) elements potas-
sium, rubidium, or cesium into low-gap (Agx,Cu1−x)(Iny,Ga1−y)(Sz,
Se1−z)2-based absorbers is standard for solar cell applications, since
highest efficiencies (η > 22%) cannot be reached if only sodium
(mandatory for decent performance) is added [1–3]. In most cases,
the HA species is supplied in the form of evaporated (HA)F in a
post absorber deposition treatment (HA-PDT), with the first report
of the beneficial effect of a potassium fluoride-post-deposition
treatment (KF-PDT) dating back to 2013 [4]. It was observed that
the HA-PDT allows growing substantially thinner CdS buffer
layers without losses in open-circuit voltage (VOC) or fill factor
(FF), resulting in higher short-circuit current densities (JSC).
Possible explanations are a facilitated Cd in-diffusion (creating
type inversion) [4, 5] and an earlier formation of a fully covering
CdS layer during chemical bath deposition (CBD) [6, 7]. Typically,
the HA-PDT also leads to higher VOC values, but the underlying
physical mechanism is still under debate [3, 8–11]. Prevalent sug-
gestions are that, after HA-PDT, the recombination rates are
reduced i) at the interface to the buffer by the formation of a very
thin, wide-gap (Alkali,Cu)-(In,Ga)-Se surface layer (possibly with-
out Ga and Cu) [12–17], ii) at grain boundaries via a reduction/
passivation of charged defects [18–20], or iii) in the grain interiors
due to a reduced concentration of deep defects [21, 22] (deemed
unlikely by others [18]). Alternative explanations are an increased
doping density [23–25] (but lower doping was observed as well
[26]) and reduced potential fluctuations [27].

absorbers with bandgap energies (EG) > 1.4 eV, as required for a
top cell in a tandem PV device [28, 29]. In case of cells based

on a pure ternary CuGaSe2 (CGS) absorber, a HA-PDT did not lead
to a significant increase in performance [15, 30, 31]. It was pro-
posed that the absence of a HA-In-Se (no indium in CuGaSe2) sur-
face phase [15] or the formation of more detrimental interface
defects [31] prevent any beneficial effect. However, a small VOC
gain was observed when RbF was added during the final stage
of absorber formation and not as a PDT [32]. Zahedi-Azad et
al. showed that a HA-PDT can lead to an improved VOC and effi-
ciency for Cu(In,Ga)Se2 (CIGS) solar cells with a [Ga]/([Ga]+[In])
ratio (GGI) up to 0.8 [33, 34]. They claim that while recombina-
tion at the CIGS/CdS interface is still limiting, it can be signifi-
cantly mitigated by the HA-PDT. However, for too large amounts
of (HA)F a transport barrier at the front contact was claimed to
lead to FF losses [33]. More recently, we tested a RbF-PDT for
(Ag,Cu) (In,Ga)Se2 (ACIGS) solar cells with a GGI ≈0.7 and
a [Ag]/([Ag]+[Cu]) ratio (AAC) of 0.5–0.7 and found a statisti-
cally significant VOC increase, leading to a top efficiency of
16.3% [35]. Photoelectron-spectroscopy measurements indicate
that CIGS surfaces with a high GGI are less modified by a
HA-PDT and no Rb-In-Se surface layer was detected after
RbF-PDT on CIGS with GGI = 0.9 [36]. All aforementioned
works are summarized in Table 1.
Overall, it can be concluded that, according to the previous inves-
tigations, the absorber should contain a sufficient (minimum)
amount of indium to utilize any beneficial effect of a HA-
PDT. In addition, similar to low-gap absorbers [37–40], the
(HA)F dose can also become too large for wide-gap CIGS films,
leading to FF deterioration [30, 33, 35].
In the present work, we investigate the effect of a RbF-PDT for Cu-
free Ag(In,Ga)Se2 (AIGS, i.e., AAC = 1) solar cells with a GGI of 0.5,
leading to EG ≈1.5 eV. As compared to previous works on wide-gap
ACIGS solar cells [35, 41–50], the Cu was removed altogether to
reach the same bandgap, but with a lower Ga content [51]. The
intention is that the lower GGI improves the absorber bulk proper-
ties (i.e., electron lifetime), as observed for Ag-free CIGS solar
cells [52–63]. Since a positive conduction-band offset (CBO) of
about + 0.35 eV is predicted at the CdS/AIGS interface for the used
absorber composition [42], interface recombination is expected to
play only a minor role, but a slightly detrimental effect on FF
may occur [64]. Up to this point, the total exclusion of Cu to process
wide-gap AIGS solar cells was barely tested before and, to the best of
our knowledge, only for GGI ≥0.8 and without HA-PDT [65–69].
To use a wide-gap A(C)IGS device as a top cell in a tandem struc-
ture, the back-contact material needs to be transparent. In the
past, different transparent conductive oxides were tested and a
concise summary of most works can be found in [48, 49]. A good
compromise between a sufficiently low sheet resistance (Rsheet)
and a high near-infrared (NIR) transparency in the final device
was achieved by using an In2O3:W (IOW) back contact [49, 50].
Thus, in this work we compare the effect of a RbF-PDT for AIGS
solar cells with standard, opaque Mo to devices with transparent
IOW back contacts, both subjected to the exact same absorber
deposition runs. In addition, a reduction of the standard CdS
thickness was evaluated for each sample, too.

Performance

PDT thicknesses (0 to 20 nm, in Se atmosphere), were conducted.

In each run, soda-lime glass (SLG) substrates coated with Mo or
IOW were added and sodium was provided by a NaF-precursor
film on top of the back contact. In the case of the transparent back
contact (TBC), the NaF addition was chosen to be lower (7 nm) as
compared to Mo (15 nm), since earlier works suggest that a NaF
thickness of ≥10 nm leads to excessive GaOx formation at the
absorber/TBC interface, resulting in FF losses [48]. To study a
potential reduction of the CdS thickness without performance
losses, as enabled by the HA-PDT for low-gap (A)CIGS solar cells,
two different CdS buffer layer thicknesses, a standard ≈65 nm
thick (‘std’) and a ≈35 nm thick (‘thin’) film, are compared for each
sample.
An overview of all samples is provided in Table 2, which lists the
corresponding integral compositions (I/III = [Ag]/ ([Ga]+[In]))
and absorber layer thicknesses (dabs), as deduced from
X-ray fluorescence (XRF) measurements, as well as the
bandgap energies, as extracted from external quantum effi-
ciency (EQE) measurements (inflection point method). As is
evident from the table, the absorber properties are very similar
in terms of composition and thickness for all samples, allowing
a fair evaluation of the effect of the RbF-PDT. Intentionally,
very close-stoichiometric AIGS compositions were targeted,
since for absorbers with AAC ≥0.5, I/III values >0.90 lead to
a significant widening of the space charge region, resulting
in adequate carrier collection, despite the low diffusion length
in wide-gap chalcopyrite material [35, 41, 44, 70, 71]. A dabs
value of ≈1.1 μm was previously identified to be optimal for
maximizing the efficiency under rear illumination, without
sacrificing too much of the performance level at front illumi-
nation [49, 50].

istics (a, b) and EQE spectra (c, d) of the best cell for each sample
with a Mo and IOW back contact, respectively. Here, we only
show the results for the thinner CdS, since the samples with
standard-thick buffers show very similar trends (see Figure S1
in supporting information). All corresponding JV parameters
can be found in Table 2, including the short-circuit current den-
sities as derived from integration of the EQE spectra (JSC,qe)
and the corresponding, spectral-mismatch and probe-shading

increasing RbF dose for all samples. The most pronounced loss is
a reduction in FF, indicating the creation of a transport barrier. It
was suggested that the excessive formation of an HA-In-Se phase

losses upon too intense HA-PDTs [8, 39, 40, 72]. Since the exclu-
sion of Cu in the used AIGS film leads to a significant downshift
of the conduction band minimum [42], an even larger CBO
would be expected at a potential RbInSe2/AIGS interface, leading
to a more detrimental transport barrier. Alternatively, it was pro-
posed that when too many Na atoms are replaced by heavier
alkalis at the back contact interface, a significant back contact
barrier establishes, explaining the FF losses [26, 73].

In each run, soda-lime glass (SLG) substrates coated with Mo or
IOW were added and sodium was provided by a NaF-precursor
film on top of the back contact. In the case of the transparent back
contact (TBC), the NaF addition was chosen to be lower (7 nm) as
compared to Mo (15 nm), since earlier works suggest that a NaF
thickness of ≥10 nm leads to excessive GaOx formation at the
absorber/TBC interface, resulting in FF losses [48]. To study a
potential reduction of the CdS thickness without performance
losses, as enabled by the HA-PDT for low-gap (A)CIGS solar cells,
two different CdS buffer layer thicknesses, a standard ≈65 nm
thick (‘std’)anda≈35 nm thick (‘thin’) film, are compared for each
sample.
An overview of all samples is provided in Table 2, which lists the
corresponding integral compositions (I/III = [Ag]/ ([Ga]+[In]))
and absorber layer thicknesses (dabs), as deduced from
X-ray fluorescence (XRF) measurements, as well as the
bandgap energies, as extracted from external quantum effi-
ciency (EQE) measurements (inflection point method). As is
evident from the table, the absorber properties are very similar
in terms of composition and thickness for all samples, allowing
a fair evaluation of the effect of the RbF-PDT. Intentionally,
very close-stoichiometric AIGS compositions were targeted,

value of ≈1.1 μm was previously identified to be optimal for
maximizing the efficiency under rear illumination, without
sacrificing too much of the performance level at front illumi-

it cannot be excluded that the total alkali concentration is just too
high after HA-PDT when an IOW back contact is used, since it
allows for only very minor alkali diffusion from the absorber
back into the SLG (in stark contrast to Mo). To clarify some
of these questions, the Rb distribution and interface modifica-
tions after RbF-PDT are illustrated and discussed later in
Section 2.2.
Only in the case of 20 nm RbF and for an IOW back contact does
the PDT-induced photocurrent blocking also result in a decreased
JSC, expressed by a constant reduction of the EQE level (see
Figure 1d). For all other samples, the EQE is not significantly
affected by the RbF-PDT or the choice of the back contact. The
reflectance (R) spectra for the samples with 10 nm RbF and Mo
are added in Figure 1c,d and S1(c,d) for full devices with thin
and standard CdS layers, respectively. Very good carrier collection
is observed for all samples, facilitated by the electrical field in the
fully depleted absorber films (see capacitance–voltage (CV) meas-
urements in Figure S2 in supporting information). Remaining
losses can be mainly attributed to parasitic absorption in the
ZnO:Al front electrode and, to a lesser extent, to transmission
losses by incomplete absorption in the AIGS film as well as absorp-
tion in ordered vacancy compounds (OVCs) at the absorber sur-
face [80]. When comparing the EQE spectra of samples with thin
and standard CdS (Figure 1c,d vs Figure S1(c,d)) it may appear as if
the collection in the NIR region is reduced in the latter case.
However, the differences in EQE in the NIR region are mainly
arising from differences in reflection losses (1-R) and R-corrected

was shown to provide very good performance [78].

VOC and FF rather improved slightly with the thinner CdS buffer,
while JSC even increased by about 1–2 mA/cm2, due to the
reduced parasitic absorption. In a previous works, we found that
our CdS deposition process leads to closed films on low-gap CIGS
absorbers for average layer thicknesses ≥30 nm, leading to no
more VOC, but a continuous FF increase for thicker films up
to the standard thickness [81]. At this point, we cannot explain
why the thinner buffer layer is clearly advantageous for the per-
formance of the AIGS solar cells analyzed in this study. In the
future, we plan to further reduce the CdS thickness to identify
the optimum configuration.
Overall, the performance level of the AIGS cells with a Mo back
contact and without HA-PDT is similar to samples which include
Cu and have the same bandgap [41, 48, 49]. Table 3 compares the
best cells from this study (AAC = 1, GGI = 0.5) with the best Cu-
containing cell from our earlier work (AAC = 0.8, GGI = 0.6) [49].
For the standard CdS thickness, the sample with Cu shows a higher
FF, but very comparable VOC and JSC values. The reason for the
lower FF for the AIGS sample in this study may be the more
pronounced CBO at the CdS interface (≈0.35 eV vs ≈0.25 eV
[42]). In summary, reducing the Ga content from GGI = 0.6 to
GGI = 0.5 for a fixed bandgap of 1.46–1.47 eV by increasing the
AAC to 1 did not result in an improved cell performance. This
questions the hypothesis that the deep GaI defect is responsible
for the large VOC deficit of wide-gap ACIGS solar cells [55–61].
Light soaking is often seen to improve the performance of (HA)F-
treated ACIGS solar cells [1, 82, 83]. However, none of the samples
in this work (with or without PDT) improved by light soaking, but
instead even showed VOC degradation after 4 weeks of storage in
ambient conditions. It is therefore advised to limit the AAC value
to ≤0.5 and accept a slightly higher GGI value for a given bandgap,
which was also shown to minimize metastability issues [70, 71].
On the contrary, the thermodynamical stability of the absorber
(i.e., also of the final cell) is predicted to decrease with increasing
Ga content and AAC values close to 0.5 [84]. Thus, an AAC ≈0.4
may be optimal, still allowing for a sufficiently wide space charge
region for close-stoichiometric absorbers, while being more stable
and potentially gaining from a RbF-PDT.

Chemical and Structural Modifications
underneath the Absorber Surface
Figure 7a,b shows the scanning transmission electron micros-
copy (STEM) cross-section images of the samples with standard
CdS and TBC without and with 20 nm RbF-PDT, respectively.
The dark spots are Ag precipitations, forming during lamella
preparation, as reported before for ACIGS solar cells [35, 44].
No significant structural changes are observed on the micrometer
scale after RbF-PDT. An open question raised in Section 2.1 was
whether the RbF-PDT leads to a thicker GaOx film at the AIGS/
IOW interface, potentially explaining the stronger FF deteriora-
tion for cells with IOW as compared to Mo. Indeed, as can be seen
in Figure 7c,d, which highly magnifies the back contact region, a
thicker GaOx layer (3.0 nm on average) is found after RbF-PDT as
compared to the sample without PDT (1.7 nm on average). The
latter value is in good agreement with our earlier work on ACIGS
with an IOW TBC [49]. However, a GaOx thickness of 3.0 nm is
still thinner as observed in other studies on (A)CIGS devices
with a TBC, which show no significant transport barrier and
high FF values for GaOx thicknesses up to at least 4 nm
[76–79]. Thus, it is deemed unlikely that the rather moderate
increase in GaOx extension from 1.7 to 3.0 nm alone explains
the strong photocurrent blocking in JV for the RbF-treated sam-
ples in this work.
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) in STEM mode was
performed at the back contact region of the sample without RbF,
see Figure S9 in supporting information. Besides confirming the
presence of the GaOx layer, the analysis shows that the grain
boundaries close to the back contact are Ag-depleted and In-
enriched (same is true for majority of analyzed grain boundaries,
independent of their location, not shown here). A depletion of
group-I elements (Ag or Cu) is frequently observed in ACIGS
random, high-angle grain boundaries [18, 35, 87, 88] and claimed
to make them electrically more benign [89]. It was found that
with increasing Ga and for GGI > 0.4, grain boundaries in
CIGS are more likely to be group-I enriched and thereby poten-
tially more detrimental. However, no such Ag-rich grain bound-
aries were identified in this study.
The same STEM-EDS analysis was conducted for the correspond-
ing sample with 20 nm RbF-PDT, as illustrated in Figure 8a,b.
Again, the grain boundaries are Ag-depleted and In-enriched,
but in this case also decorated by rubidium. It was suggested that
the introduction of Rb leads to a slightly more pronounced (or fre-
quent) group-I depletion in CIGS grain boundaries [18, 87, 88],
which cannot be confirmed nor excluded in the present study.
We further find that Rb is also located at the AIGS/GaOx/IOW
interface of our samples. Extracted absolute and normalized
([0,1]) EDS line-scans across the back interface, presented in

4 | Experimental Section
4.1 | Solar cell processing
A stack of SLG/(Mo or IOW)/NaF/AIGS/CdS/ZnO:Al was
used for the solar cell samples in this work. The opaque Mo
back contact (320 nm, Rsheet ≈0.7 Ω sq−1) was direct-current
sputtered, while IOW (300-380 nm, Rsheet ≈10 Ω sq−1) was
radio-frequency sputtered from an In2O3-WO3 compound target
(nominally 1 wt.% WO3) in an Ar (40 sccm) and O2 (0.4 sccm)
gas mixture. Sodium in-diffusion from the SLG was allowed
(no alkali diffusion-barrier), but additionally 7 nm- (for IOW)
or 15 nm-thick (for Mo) NaF precursor layers were coated on
top of the back electrodes via thermal evaporation. Next, a
three-stage (Ag-poor →Ag-rich →Ag-poor) co-evaporation
process was applied to grow ≈1.1 μm thick AIGS films at a
maximum substrate temperature of T = 550°C (≈3 min at
T > 500°C). Higher Ga and lower In rates in the initial growth
stages led to the formation of a bandgap grading toward the
back contact (see also Figure S10 in the supporting informa-
tion). For samples subjected to a RbF-PDT, the metal sources
were then switched off and RbF was deposited at T ≈350°C
for different times at a rate of ≈1 nm/min in Se-containing
atmosphere. In total, 4 AIGS depositions with different RbF

Advanced material characterization reveals that the RbF-PDT-

However, most grain boundaries are also found to be Ag-depleted

We further propose that the desired VOC boost is absent for AIGS
solar cells, since the Rb incorporation does not lead to a doping
increase for close-stoichiometric Cu-free absorbers, which
remain fully depleted, independent of a PDT step. The possible
explanation may be the higher alkali solubility in the chalcopy-

was not expected anyhow, due to a favorable band alignment of
the untreated AIGS absorber with the CdS buffer layer. Overall,
this work shows that a RbF-PDT is not suitable for wide-gap
AIGS solar cells, especially when a transparent back contact
is used.

4.3 | Electro-optical characterization of solar cells
The EQE (only best cell each) and JV (all cells per sample) meas-
urements of completed solar cells were conducted in home-built
setups. To avoid any reflection from the stage surfaces, a highly
absorbing, black sponge was placed underneath the solar cells
with IOW. The JV characteristics were measured in forward
V-sweep at a temperature of 25°C under illumination by a class
AAA solar simulator from G2V (Pico), using light emitting diode
(LED) arrays. The light intensity was adjusted to match the JSC
value at 1 sun irradiance of a calibrated Si reference solar cell.

Agilent 4284A precision LCR meter and a Keithley 2401 source
meter. A dielectric constant of εr = 10 was assumed for the AIGS
